body:
Childhood & Early Life

John Milton was born on Bread Street in London on December 9, 1608, in a house that sat under the sign of the Spread Eagle. His father was a scrivener, which is part lawyer, part money-lender, and also a gifted composer, so the house was full of music from the start. The family was comfortable and the boy was clearly the one they were betting on. He was reading late into the night from a young age, and later said that his eyes started to fail from it. A tutor came to the house, then St Paul's School, then Christ's College, Cambridge, where he was so slight and so fastidious that other students called him "the Lady of Christ's." He did not take it as a joke. He fell out with a tutor, was sent home for a while, and came back with a chip on his shoulder that never entirely left.

He left Cambridge with a Master's degree and the family expectation that he would become a clergyman. He refused. He had decided, privately and with enormous seriousness, that he was going to be a great poet. For almost six years he lived at his father's country house and simply read: Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Italian, history, theology, everything. He treated his own life as a long preparation for one huge work.

What He Did & Why He's Remembered

Milton wrote Paradise Lost, the epic of the Fall, in twelve books of blank verse, and it is still the great English epic. Its central problem is that the most magnetic character in it is the Devil. Satan has the best speeches, the wounded pride, the refusal to bow, and generations of readers have been uncomfortable about how much they enjoy him. William Blake said Milton was "of the Devil's party without knowing it." Whether Milton knew it or not is one of the best arguments in literature.

He was also a political writer, and a dangerous one. He argued for divorce on the grounds of incompatibility, against censorship, and eventually in defence of the execution of a king. In 1644 he published Areopagitica, a speech against licensing books, which is still one of the foundational defences of a free press. In it he wrote that "he who destroys a good book, kills reason itself, kills the image of God, as it were in the eye." He meant it very literally.

Family Life

Milton was a husband and a father in a way that was messy and, for the three daughters who survived him, often hard. After his daughters were old enough he had them read aloud to him in languages they did not understand, since he was by then blind and wanted books read in Greek and Latin. The daughters reportedly resented it. One of them, Deborah, later said her father was a delightful man to talk to, which is a sentence that is both kind and carefully worded.

His own father lived with him in his later years. His mother died in 1637, and Milton wrote of her only briefly. His friend Edward King drowned in 1637, and Milton answered with Lycidas, a pastoral elegy that is half grief and half terror at dying before he had written anything.

Romantic Life

In 1642, at 33, Milton married 17-year-old Mary Powell, the daughter of a royalist family. Within weeks she went home to her parents for what was supposed to be a short visit, and did not come back. Milton, humiliated and furious, wrote a series of pamphlets arguing that a marriage with no meeting of minds should be dissolvable. It was scandalous, and he was denounced for it. In 1645 Mary came back, and he took her in. They had four children, and she died in 1652 after the birth of their third daughter.

In 1656 he married Katherine Woodcock, and by every account was very happy. She died in 1658, a few months after giving birth to a daughter who also died. He never saw her face, because he was already blind. That is what the sonnet below is about. In 1663 he married Elizabeth Minshull, who was about thirty years younger, and who looked after him until he died.

Life Until Death

By 1652 Milton was completely blind. He had lost sight in one eye years earlier and he went on working as Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Council of State under Cromwell, writing letters in Latin to the courts of Europe, with assistants doing the reading and writing. He believed that his sight was lost in the cause of his country and he never took it back.

The Restoration of Charles II in 1660 was a disaster for him. His books were burned, he went into hiding, was arrested, and by a stroke of luck and some friends in Parliament, he was not executed. He lived the rest of his life in a smaller house, blind, in poverty, writing the poem he had been preparing for since his twenties. He dictated it to whoever was available: his daughters, friends, young men who came to be his eyes.

Paradise Lost was published in 1667. The publisher paid him £10. He lived to see a second edition in 12 books, followed by Paradise Regained and the tragedy Samson Agonistes, in which a blind hero pulls down the temple of his enemies. He died on November 8 or 9, 1674, probably of gout, and was buried at St Giles Cripplegate.

His Works

Paradise Lost, Book I. The opening

Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit
Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste
Brought death into the World, and all our woe,
With loss of Eden, till one greater Man
Restore us, and regain the blissful seat,
Sing, Heavenly Muse, that, on the secret top
Of Oreb, or of Sinai, didst inspire
That shepherd who first taught the chosen seed
In the beginning how the heavens and earth
Rose out of Chaos: or, if Sion hill
Delight thee more, and Siloa’s brook that flowed
Fast by the oracle of God, I thence
Invoke thy aid to my adventurous song,
That with no middle flight intends to soar
Above th’ Aonian mount, while it pursues
Things unattempted yet in prose or rhyme.
And chiefly thou, O Spirit, that dost prefer
Before all temples th’ upright heart and pure,
Instruct me, for thou know’st; thou from the first
Wast present, and, with mighty wings outspread,
Dove-like sat’st brooding on the vast Abyss,
And mad’st it pregnant: what in me is dark
Illumine, what is low raise and support;
That, to the height of this great argument,
I may assert Eternal Providence,
And justify the ways of God to men.

Paradise Lost, Book I. Satan, newly fallen, looks at Hell

“Is this the region, this the soil, the clime,”
Said then the lost Archangel, “this the seat
That we must change for Heaven?—this mournful gloom
For that celestial light? Be it so, since he
Who now is sovereign can dispose and bid
What shall be right: farthest from him is best
Whom reason hath equalled, force hath made supreme
Above his equals. Farewell, happy fields,
Where joy for ever dwells! Hail, horrors! hail,
Infernal world! and thou, profoundest Hell,
Receive thy new possessor—one who brings
A mind not to be changed by place or time.
The mind is its own place, and in itself
Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.
What matter where, if I be still the same,
And what I should be, all but less than he
Whom thunder hath made greater? Here at least
We shall be free; th’ Almighty hath not built
Here for his envy, will not drive us hence:
Here we may reign secure; and, in my choice,
To reign is worth ambition, though in Hell:
Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.
But

"The mind is its own place" is the line everyone quotes. Read it again and notice that it is also what a person says when they have lost everything and refuse to feel it.

Paradise Lost, Book XII. The last lines

Sonnet XIX, "When I consider how my light is spent"

When I consider how my light is spent,
Ere half my days, in this dark world and wide,
And that one Talent which is death to hide
Lodged with me useless, though my Soul more bent
To serve therewith my Maker, and present
My true account, lest he returning chide;
"Doth God exact day-labour, light denied?"
I fondly ask. But Patience, to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, "God doth not need
Either man's work or his own gifts: who best
Bear his mild yoke, they serve him best. His state
Is Kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed
And post o'er Land and Ocean without rest:
They also serve who only stand and wait."

Sonnet XXIII, "Methought I saw my late espoused Saint"

Methought I saw my late espoused Saint
Brought to me like Alcestis from the grave,
Whom Jove's great Son to her glad Husband gave,
Rescu'd from death by force though pale and faint.
Mine as whom washt from spot of child-bed taint,
Purification in the Old Law did save,
And such, as yet once more I trust to have
Full sight of her in Heaven without restraint,
Came vested all in white, pure as her mind:
Her face was veil'd, yet to my fancied sight,
Love, sweetness, goodness, in her person shin'd
So clear, as in no face with more delight.
But O as to embrace me she enclin'd
I wak'd, she fled, and day brought back my night.

The last line of that sonnet is the one to read twice. He dreamed his dead wife was finally standing in front of him, and woke up before she touched him. "Day brought back my night" is a man describing waking up blind and widowed in a single phrase.

Areopagitica (1644)

I cannot praise a fugitive and cloistered virtue, unexercised and unbreathing, that never sallies out and sees her adversary, but slinks out of the race where that immortal garland is to be run for, not without dust and heat.
epi: the blind poet who gave the Devil the best lines
